metadata.title: Inductive and combinatorial reasoning in international educational context: assessment, measurement invariance, and latent mean differences

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used an online eDia platform to administer inductive reasoning (IR) and combinatorial reasoning (CR) tests plus a learning-strategies questionnaire to Indonesian and Hungarian students in two grade levels (8th and 11th). The analytic sample was created by excluding Indonesian students with more than 80% missing data on any measure, and by using a cleaned Hungarian sample after data cleaning; no sampling-weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is reported in the provided text. Because the analysis is based on multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA) and SEM in Mplus (rather than ML prediction), the manuscript does not describe applying complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures. For replication with ILSA-style microdata, analysts should use the dataset’s provided sampling weights if available and ensure that missingness handling and group comparisons are consistent with the weight-aware estimation approach; here, the paper’s weighting strategy is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are latent constructs (IR and CR) estimated via confirmatory factor analysis/SEM using test items and a J-index for CR, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA framework. Missing data handling is described for the Indonesian sample via exclusion of students with more than 80% missingness on any measure, so a PV/missing-data imputation strategy for PVs is not relevant to this study design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were randomly drawn from 8th to 11th grades in Indonesian and Hungarian public primary and secondary schools. For Indonesia, although 345 students initially participated, students were excluded from all analyses if they had more than 80% missing data on any of the measures; the final Indonesian analytic sample comprised 250 students (56 in 8th grade, 194 in 11th grade). For Hungary, 864 students were available for analyses after data cleaning, and the authors also used randomly selected subjects from the Hungarian sample based on demographic data; gender ratios were matched between countries. The IR and CR analyses used only anchoring items common across language versions (IR: 25 anchoring items; CR: 7 anchoring items).

main_findings.dataset_used: IR and CR reasoning tests (online eDia), Indonesia vs Hungary; Grade 8 and Grade 11; inductive reasoning (IR) latent construct
main_findings.performance_metrics: Measurement invariance (MGCFA): across nationalities—acceptable fit; strong factorial invariance for IR (CFI=.926, TLI=.952, RMSEA=.055). Latent mean comparisons: Indonesia 8th vs 11th—similar (MIDN_8=0; MIDN_11=-.02, SE=.05, p>.05). Cross-national grade comparison: 8th grade—Indonesia similar to Hungary (MIDN_8=.02; MHUN_8=0, SE=.01, p>.05); 11th grade—Indonesia worse than Hungary (MIDN_11=-.25; MHUN_11=0, SE=.08, p<.01). SEM predictive paths: control strategies predict IR in Indonesia (β=.46, p<.01); IR and CR correlated (IDN r=.51, p<.01; HUN r=.56, p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using IR and CR reasoning tests (online eDia) data from Indonesia and Hungary (Grades 8 and 11), the study leveraged learning strategies—especially control strategies—along with the latent IR construct to analyze inductive reasoning achievement, finding that Indonesian IR did not improve sufficiently from Grade 8 to Grade 11 and that Indonesian students were significantly lower than Hungarian peers in Grade 11. This indicates that strengthening metacognitive control-oriented learning strategy instruction may help support higher-order reasoning development, particularly after early secondary schooling, though the study is correlational/structural rather than causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: IR and CR reasoning tests (online eDia), Indonesia vs Hungary; Grade 8 and Grade 11; combinatorial reasoning (CR) latent construct
main_findings.performance_metrics: Measurement invariance (MGCFA): across nationalities—partial invariance; strict factorial invariance failed for CR (CFI=.898, TLI=.881, RMSEA=.104). Across grades: Indonesia—strong factorial invariance held (CFI=1.000, TLI=1.000, RMSEA=.000); Hungary—measurement invariance across grades failed (CFI=.933, TLI=.892, RMSEA=.104 for configural; strict factorial also failed). Latent mean comparisons: Indonesia 8th vs 11th—11th slightly but significantly lower (MIDN_8=0; MIDN_11=-.07, SE=.03, p<.05). Cross-national grade comparison: 8th grade—Indonesia similar to Hungary (MIDN_8=.02; MHUN_8=0, SE=.01, p>.05); 11th grade—Indonesia worse than Hungary (MIDN_11=-.29; MHUN_11=0, SE=.03, p<.001). SEM predictive paths: elaboration strategies predict CR in Hungary (β=.18, p<.05); memorization strategies not significant in either model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using IR and CR reasoning tests (online eDia) data from Indonesia and Hungary (Grades 8 and 11), the study leveraged learning strategies—especially elaboration strategies—to analyze combinatorial reasoning achievement, finding that Indonesian CR did not develop between Grade 8 and Grade 11 and that Indonesian students were significantly lower than Hungarian peers in Grade 11 but not in Grade 8. This indicates that curriculum and teaching approaches that explicitly foster elaboration (linking new material to prior knowledge and real-life contexts) may be particularly important for improving combinatorial reasoning outcomes, while cross-grade comparisons are constrained by partial measurement invariance.

data.outcome_summary: The study compares inductive reasoning (IR) and combinatorial reasoning (CR) development between Indonesian and Hungarian students using online eDia assessments administered in two sessions (CR + learning strategies, then IR) to Grades 8 and 11. The analytic sample comprised 250 Indonesian students and 864 Hungarian students after excluding Indonesian cases with >80% missingness and applying data cleaning in Hungary. Measurement invariance was evaluated with multi-group confirmatory factor analysis in Mplus: IR showed strong invariance across nationalities and grades (in both countries), while CR showed partial invariance across nationalities and failed across grades in Hungary. Latent mean comparisons indicated stagnation for Indonesian reasoning skills from Grade 8 to 11 and a Grade-11 disadvantage versus Hungary for both IR and CR. Learning strategies were modeled via SEM: control strategies predicted IR in Indonesia (β=.46, p<.01), and elaboration strategies predicted CR in Hungary (β=.18, p<.05), with memorization not significant. The study does not use PV-based achievement or ML prediction; therefore, causal claims about strategy effects are limited.
